page.title: NYC Boundaries — KnoEdg.NYC
page.description: Why New York City can have several valid borough and county boundaries, and what those different boundary views mean.

content.text: New York City does not have just one useful boundary map. Different publishers draw or describe the same five boroughs differently depending on whether the question is about shoreline, surrounding water, counties, administrative relations or gazetteer identity.

children.alt: Overlay comparing water-included boundaries in blue with water-excluded shoreline geometry in green for New York City’s five boroughs

caption.text: Water excluded DCP boundary-method overlay · five boroughs

content.text: A boundary depends on the question being asked. The Department of City Planning publishes both water-excluded shoreline geometry and water-included geometry. The Census Bureau publishes county land and water measurements. OpenStreetMap represents each borough and its corresponding county as separate administrative relations, even where they refer to the same real-world extent. geoBoundaries republishes generalized, shoreline-clipped Census-derived county geometry; Overture Maps integrates the exact OpenStreetMap relation versions already governed here while adding stable division and area identifiers. Who's On First adds stable gazetteer identifiers, hierarchy and concordances for the five counties; its default county geometry is a Census-sourced Quattroshapes derivative.
These are not interchangeable records. This view keeps the source, method, administrative framing and review assessment attached to each claim.
The two independent, directly comparable land-area series are within 1.25% for every borough/county pair; this is treated as ordinary cross-source measurement variance, not a contradiction.

Other representations can still be useful without counting as independent corroboration. The technical collection keeps each source's method, provenance relationship and review assessment attached to the record.
